title: From Java source to a running program
summary: Follow a Java file through compilation and JVM execution, then learn to separate compiler failures from runtime failures.
outcomes: Explain the distinct responsibilities of the JDK, javac, bytecode and JVM.
Compile and run a Java 17 console program using repeatable commands.
Classify a failure as source, compilation or runtime related.
Read a compiler message and make one evidence-based repair.

briefing.story: The Student Registration campaign begins with an empty console. Before building students, repositories or APIs, you must understand how a readable Java file becomes instructions a computer can execute.
briefing.purpose: A learner who understands the build-and-run path can diagnose errors instead of treating the IDE as a magic Run button.
briefing.mentalModel: Think of source code as a recipe written for developers. javac checks and translates that recipe into bytecode, a standard package of instructions. A JVM installed for a particular operating system reads that package and executes it.

prerequisites.name: File
prerequisites.explanation: A named piece of information stored on a computer. Java source files conventionally end in .java.

prerequisites.name: Command
prerequisites.explanation: An instruction entered in a terminal or triggered by an IDE, such as compile or run.

prerequisites.name: Program
prerequisites.explanation: A set of instructions arranged to produce behaviour when executed.

terms.meaning: The Java Development Kit: the compiler, launcher and other tools required to build Java software.
terms.example: The javac command is supplied by the JDK.

terms.meaning: A program that checks source code and translates it into another representation.
terms.example: javac StudentApp.java creates StudentApp.class when compilation succeeds.

terms.meaning: The platform-neutral instructions stored in a Java class file.
terms.example: StudentApp.class contains bytecode rather than editable Java source.

terms.meaning: The Java Virtual Machine that loads, verifies and executes bytecode on a particular system.
terms.example: java StudentApp starts a JVM and asks it to run StudentApp.

terms.meaning: The method where a console application's execution begins.
terms.example: public static void main(String[] args) is the entry point used here.

misconceptions.belief: The JVM directly understands the text inside a .java file.
misconceptions.correction: The normal path compiles source into bytecode first; the JVM loads the resulting class.

misconceptions.belief: If compilation succeeds, the program cannot fail.
misconceptions.correction: Compilation proves syntax and type rules, not every runtime input or behaviour.

briefing.readinessCheck: In your own words, name the artifact before compilation, the artifact after compilation and the component that executes the compiled artifact.

demonstration.title: Register the first hunter
demonstration.introduction: This complete one-file application is intentionally small. Its job is to prove the toolchain before domain complexity is introduced.
runInstructions: Open a terminal in the src directory.
Run javac StudentRegistrationApp.java and confirm that StudentRegistrationApp.class appears.
Run java StudentRegistrationApp without adding .class to the command.
Repeat the run from the IDE and confirm that both routes produce the same output.
demonstration.expectedOutput:
Registration system online
Candidate STU-101: Ravi
executionFlow: javac reads StudentRegistrationApp.java and checks syntax and types.
Successful compilation produces StudentRegistrationApp.class containing bytecode.
The java launcher starts a JVM and loads the StudentRegistrationApp class.
The JVM invokes main, creates two String values and calls the output methods.

training.workspace: Use Java 17 in IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code, Eclipse or a terminal. Keep the source file and generated class file visible during the first two steps.

steps.title: Prove the source-to-bytecode transition
steps.goal: See that source and compiled output are separate artifacts.
steps.why: This distinction explains why compilation errors occur before program execution.
steps.action: Delete any old .class file, run javac StudentRegistrationApp.java and inspect the directory.
steps.observe: A new StudentRegistrationApp.class file appears and the application has not printed anything yet.
steps.ifItFails: If javac is not recognized, verify that a Java 17 JDK—not only an editor—is installed and configured.
steps.checkpoint: You can point to the editable source and compiled bytecode as two different files.

steps.title: Execute the compiled class
steps.goal: Start the JVM and run the entry point.
steps.why: Running is a different operation from compiling.
steps.observe: The two expected lines appear without creating a new source file.
steps.ifItFails: If Java reports that it cannot find the main class, confirm the current directory, class name and capitalization.
steps.checkpoint: Your console output exactly matches the demonstration output.

steps.title: Create a compile-time failure
steps.goal: Learn to read a compiler message without guessing.
steps.why: Compiler feedback normally names a location, an expected type and the incompatible value.
steps.action: Temporarily change String studentId to int studentId while leaving the text value unchanged, then compile.
steps.observe: javac reports an incompatible-types error and no new runnable class is produced from the broken source.
steps.ifItFails: If the application still runs, you may be executing the older .class file. Compilation and execution are separate; inspect timestamps or delete the old class file.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the source line and explain why text cannot be assigned to an int.

steps.title: Repair and verify
steps.goal: Close the debugging loop with evidence.
steps.why: A repair is complete only after compilation and execution both succeed.
steps.action: Restore String studentId, compile again and run the application.
steps.observe: Compilation succeeds and the original output returns.
steps.ifItFails: Read the first compiler error, fix only that issue and compile again before changing anything else.
steps.checkpoint: The program compiles from the repaired source and produces the expected output.

breakRepair.breakAction: Rename the class to RegistrationConsole without renaming the file, then compile.
breakRepair.symptom: javac reports that a public class must be declared in a file with the matching name.
breakRepair.repair: Rename the file to RegistrationConsole.java or restore the original public class name, then compile and run using the matching name.
breakRepair.lesson: Java's public top-level class and source filename convention is part of how tools locate code consistently.

pauseAndExplain.prompt: What does javac produce when compilation succeeds?
What happens between entering java StudentRegistrationApp and seeing the first output line?
How is a compiler error different from a runtime exception?
What happens if the source changes but you run an older class file without compiling again?

coreRules: Compile after source changes before trusting execution output.
Treat the first useful error as evidence; avoid making several speculative changes at once.
Use Java 17 consistently across the IDE, terminal and project configuration.
Do not commit generated .class files into normal source control.
useCases: Diagnosing why code works in an IDE but fails in a terminal or build pipeline.
Separating syntax/type problems from failures caused by runtime data.
Explaining Java's portability model without claiming bytecode is native machine code.
avoidWhen: Do not use manual javac commands as the permanent build strategy for a multi-module enterprise application; build tools will later coordinate dependencies, tests and packaging.
advantages: The compilation boundary catches many errors before execution.
Bytecode allows the same compiled representation to run on compatible JVM implementations.
costs: The JDK, project and runtime versions must be aligned.
Stale compiled output can confuse beginners when source changes are not recompiled.

alternatives.chooseWhen: You want convenient compilation, execution and debugging during development.
alternatives.tradeOff: The IDE can hide the underlying commands unless you inspect its configuration.

alternatives.chooseWhen: The project has dependencies, tests, packaging or multiple modules.
alternatives.tradeOff: Build tools add configuration that should be introduced after the basic toolchain is understood.

mistakes.symptom: java cannot find or load the main class.
mistakes.cause: Wrong directory, classpath, package or capitalization.
mistakes.correction: Confirm the compiled file location, package name and exact class name before changing code.

mistakes.symptom: Old output appears after source was edited.
mistakes.cause: The changed source was not compiled or an old class was executed.
mistakes.correction: Clean the generated class, compile the intended file and verify timestamps or build output.

interviewRecall.question: What is the difference between JDK, JVM and bytecode?
interviewRecall.answer: The JDK supplies development tools including javac; javac produces bytecode; a JVM loads and executes that bytecode on a particular platform.

quest.scenario: The academy needs a console status card for its first Student Management build. A user should be able to compile it, run it and confirm which Java runtime is active.
quest.currentState: You have a working Java 17 environment and the demonstration application. The quest starts in a new file so you must reproduce the toolchain independently.
requirements: Create SystemStatus.java with a valid main method.
Declare academyName and campaignName as descriptive String variables.
Read the active Java version using System.getProperty("java.version").
Print three labelled lines: academy, campaign and Java runtime.
constraints: Use only Java 17 standard-library functionality and one source file.
Do not hard-code the runtime version text.
The source filename and public class name must match.
acceptanceCriteria: javac SystemStatus.java completes without a compiler error.
java SystemStatus prints exactly three labelled, non-empty lines.
The runtime line reflects the environment value returned by Java.
A second learner can reproduce the result from your commands.
nonGoals: No user input, database, Spring annotation or multi-file design is required.
hints: System.getProperty accepts a property name and returns its value as text.
Compile first with javac SystemStatus.java, then run with java SystemStatus.
expectedBehaviour: The first two lines identify LevelCraft and the Student Registration campaign.
The third line reports the actual Java runtime rather than a manually typed version.

evidence.instructions: Paste your source code and the three output lines, then explain in one sentence which tool compiled the source and which component executed the result.

instructions: Confirm all four acceptance criteria manually.
Compare the runtime value with java -version.
Record both the successful compile command and run command in the evidence.

trial.explainPrompt: A teammate edits a message in SystemStatus.java, runs java SystemStatus immediately and still sees the old message. Explain the most likely cause and the correct recovery sequence.
trial.question: Which component normally executes the bytecode stored in a compiled Java class file?
trial.explanation: javac compiles source into bytecode. The JVM loads, verifies and executes the resulting class.

debrief.capability: You can independently compile, run and diagnose a basic Java 17 program.
debrief.applicationEvolution: The Student Management campaign now has a verified execution environment and its first runnable status program.
debrief.tradeOff: IDE automation is convenient, but understanding the underlying compiler and runtime makes tool failures diagnosable.
debrief.nextMission: J0.2 introduces the IDE workbench, packages, breakpoints and stack-trace navigation.
debrief.reflection: Which part of your normal IDE Run action was invisible to you before this mission?
